meta.title: Data Platform: Lake and Warehouse
meta.summary: A retailer's analytics platform: clickstream events streamed and orders captured by CDC into an Iceberg lake with raw, cleaned and curated zones, transformed by scheduled Spark and dbt jobs behind quality gates, and served to BI dashboards from a warehouse.

functional: Collect clickstream events (page views, searches, add to cart, checkout steps) from the web and mobile apps
Capture every insert, update and delete in the operational orders database without slowing it down
Ingest daily exports from third-party SaaS tools (ad platforms, CRM, customer support)
Keep data in three zones in object storage: raw (as received, for replay), cleaned (typed, deduplicated, PII tokenized) and curated (business tables and aggregates)
Serve BI dashboards and ad hoc SQL from a warehouse, and give data scientists Spark and SQL access to the lake
Block data that fails quality checks from reaching curated tables, and support backfills of any past day or hour
Column-level access control, PII masking and lineage from source field to dashboard
nonFunctional: Clickstream dashboards are no more than 30 minutes behind real time
Yesterday's orders and revenue tables are published by 06:00 ET every day
No event the collector acknowledged is lost; reprocessing never double counts
Events up to 3 days late (offline mobile apps) land in the correct hour
Survives the loss of one availability zone; the collector keeps accepting events even when everything behind Kafka is down

scale.label: Clickstream events
scale.value: 2B / day, about 23k / s on average and 80k / s at sale peaks, about 1 KB each

scale.label: Data landed per day
scale.value: About 2.1 TB uncompressed (2 TB clickstream, 50 GB orders CDC from 40M row changes, 20 GB SaaS exports); about 250 GB as compressed Parquet

scale.label: Retention
scale.value: Kafka 7 days; raw 13 months; cleaned 2 years; curated 7 years (finance). About 400 TB in the lake, 60% of it in infrequent-access tiers

scale.label: Warehouse
scale.value: 40 TB compressed; 600 dashboard users, up to 2k queries / hour at the Monday morning peak; 50 data scientists

scale.label: Freshness
scale.value: Clickstream dashboards within 30 min; daily finance tables by 06:00 ET

scale.label: Late events
scale.value: About 2% arrive more than 1 hour late, almost all within 3 days

slos.name: Clickstream dashboards are fresh
slos.sli: 5-minute samples where the newest hour published in the warehouse clickstream marts is less than the threshold behind now, divided by all samples

slos.name: Daily finance tables on time
slos.sli: Days on which fct_orders and daily_revenue for the previous day were published, with tests passing, by the deadline, divided by all days

slos.name: Curated data is right first time
slos.sli: Curated partitions published that did not need a restatement within 30 days, divided by all curated partitions published

slos.name: Dashboard queries are fast
slos.sli: Queries from the BI tool's service account that finish under the threshold, divided by all of them, measured in the warehouse query log

alerts.when: Newest published clickstream hour more than 30 min behind for 3 consecutive samples (15 min)
alerts.why: Merchandisers are steering a live sale on numbers that are no longer current.

alerts.when: At 04:30 ET the nightly DAG's remaining critical path, at its usual task durations, ends after 06:00 ET
alerts.why: Finance and the morning revenue email depend on it. Paging at 04:30 leaves time to rerun a failed task or scale out before the deadline.

alerts.when: BI queries slower than 5 s above 5% of queries for 15 minutes during business hours
alerts.why: Dashboards time out for hundreds of users at once.

alerts.when: Any quality gate blocks a curated publish, or more than 0.5% of a topic's events go to quarantine for 15 minutes
alerts.why: The gate already protected the dashboards, so nothing is wrong yet. Someone must find the cause and backfill before the data goes stale; if they do not, freshness-burn pages.

alerts.when: Consumer lag of the streaming job on clickstream.raw above 10 minutes of data for 10 minutes
alerts.why: The landing job is falling behind, which eats the 30 minute freshness budget before anyone sees stale dashboards.

alerts.when: CDC replication lag above 15 minutes, or WAL retained by the replication slot on the orders DB above 20 GB
alerts.why: A stalled CDC task makes the slot keep WAL on the production database. Left alone it fills the disk and takes checkout down, so act well before that.

signals.name: Quarantined events by schema
signals.why: A jump on one schema_ref points straight at the app release that broke the contract.

signals.name: Late events by delay
signals.why: Received time minus event time. Shows whether the 3 day watermark still covers almost all late events.

signals.name: Small files per partition
signals.why: Minute-by-minute streaming commits create many small files. If compaction falls behind, every query and job reading the table slows down.

signals.name: Replication slot retained WAL
signals.why: Measured on the orders DB itself: the earliest sign that CDC has stalled.

signals.name: Bytes scanned per day by team
signals.why: Query cost is mostly bytes scanned, so one dashboard or notebook without a partition filter shows up here first.

signals.name: Nightly DAG critical path end time
signals.why: Predicts the 06:00 deadline from the tasks still to run, so a slow night is visible before it becomes a late one.

steps: Find the last stage that moved: newest hour in the warehouse mart, newest snapshot on curated.page_views_hourly, newest snapshot on cleaned.events, consumer lag on clickstream.raw.
If Kafka lag is growing, check the streaming job: is it running, are micro-batches slower than the 1 minute trigger, is it stuck on one hot partition.
If cleaned is current but curated is not, open the latest curated run in the scheduler: a blocked quality gate means bad data upstream, so look at quarantine counts by schema.
If curated is current but the warehouse is not, check the load task and warehouse queueing; a load waiting behind heavy ad hoc queries needs its own workload queue.

debug.symptom: Yesterday's revenue in the dashboard does not match the orders database
steps: Compare row counts and sums for the day at each hop: orders DB, CDC change files in raw, cleaned.orders, fct_orders.
If raw is short, check the CDC task for errors or restarts and whether the nightly sensor ran before the CDC watermark passed midnight.
If cleaned differs from raw, look for changes applied out of order: the merge must keep the last change per order by LSN, not by file arrival.
If only the mart differs, check time zones (UTC in the lake, ET in finance reports) and refunds dated on a different day from the order.

nodes.label: Storefront Apps
nodes.description: Web and mobile apps with a tracking SDK that buffers events on the device and sends them in batches

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the collector hostname at the load balancer

nodes.label: Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: TLS termination and HTTP routing to the collectors

nodes.label: Event Collector
nodes.description: Deliberately thin: checks the app key and size, stamps received time, writes to Kafka. No schema validation, so a bad release never makes it reject events

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.description: The operational database behind checkout: customers, orders, order lines, refunds. The platform reads its change log, never its tables

nodes.label: Data Lake
nodes.description: Iceberg tables in Parquet, in raw, cleaned and curated zones (plus quarantine). Lifecycle rules move older files to infrequent-access tiers

nodes.label: Warehouse
nodes.description: Serves BI: dbt models and marts, partitioned and clustered, reading curated lake tables as external tables. Column masking and row policies for PII

nodes.label: Catalog and Schema Registry
nodes.description: Table metadata and Iceberg snapshot pointers, event schemas with compatibility rules, data contracts for SaaS exports, column tags (PII) that drive access policies, and lineage

nodes.label: Clickstream Topic
nodes.description: Kafka topic clickstream.raw: 96 partitions keyed by session id, replication factor 3, 7 day retention for replay

nodes.label: CDC Replication
nodes.description: Reads the orders DB's logical replication slot and writes every change, deletes included, as Parquet files to the raw zone

nodes.label: Orchestrator
nodes.description: Airflow DAGs: the 15 minute curated build, the nightly orders DAG, dbt runs and backfills. Owns dependencies, retries and SLAs

nodes.label: Spark Jobs
nodes.description: One long-running streaming job lands clickstream every minute; batch jobs on transient clusters build cleaned and curated tables, run quality gates and backfills. Checkpoints live in the lake, so a job restarts in another zone

nodes.label: SaaS Exports
nodes.description: Ad platforms, CRM and support tools; pulled daily through their export APIs, with rate limits and their own schema changes

nodes.label: BI Tool
nodes.description: Dashboards and ad hoc exploration; queries the warehouse as a service account with each user's identity passed through for access policies

flows.title: A clickstream event reaches a dashboard
flows.summary: The collector only acknowledges what Kafka has durably stored. A streaming job lands events every minute into raw and cleaned Iceberg tables by event time; every 15 minutes a batch job rebuilds the touched hours of curated tables behind a quality gate, and the warehouse replaces those hours in its marts.

steps.label: resolve events.shop.example
steps.detail: The SDK finds the collector by name, so the load balancer can change without an app release.

steps.label: POST /v1/events (batch of 20)
steps.detail: The SDK buffers events on the device and sends every 10 s or 20 events, which saves battery and requests. Each event carries its own id, schema reference and the device's event time, because the time it is sent can be hours later.

steps.label: forward
steps.detail: Collectors are stateless and spread over three zones, so any instance can take any batch.

steps.label: check key and size, stamp received_at
steps.detail: The collector does as little as possible so it stays available: no schema checks and no lookups. received_at is the server's clock, used later to measure lateness and to find which hours a backfill must touch.

steps.label: produce, key = session_id, acks=all
steps.detail: Keying by session keeps one session's events in order on one partition. acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 means an acknowledged event is on two brokers in two zones before the app is told it can drop it.

steps.label: streaming job reads (1 min trigger)
steps.detail: A Spark Structured Streaming job reads a minute of offsets at a time. Its offsets are saved in a checkpoint in the lake and committed with the table write, so a restart neither skips nor duplicates a micro-batch.

steps.label: get schema add_to_cart/3
steps.detail: Each event names its schema version; the job fetches unknown versions once and caches them, so the registry is not on the per-event path.

steps.label: validate, dedupe, partition by event time
steps.detail: Events are written to the hour they happened in, not the hour they arrived, so an event from a phone that was offline for a day lands in yesterday's partition. Duplicates from SDK retries are dropped on event_id within a 3 day watermark; events later than that go to a late table that the nightly job merges. user_id is replaced by a keyed hash in cleaned, so the raw zone is the only place it appears in clear.

steps.label: append raw + cleaned (Iceberg commit)
steps.detail: Raw keeps every event exactly as received, including ones that fail validation, so any later bug can be fixed by replaying from raw. Each Iceberg commit is atomic: readers see the whole micro-batch or none of it.
steps.payload:
-- one micro-batch, committed as a new snapshot on each table
INSERT INTO raw.clickstream      -- event_id, received_at, schema_ref, payload (string)
INSERT INTO cleaned.events       -- typed columns, PARTITIONED BY (event_type, hours(event_ts))
-- touched hours recorded for the curated build:
{ "batch": 88121, "hours": ["2026-11-10T14", "2026-11-10T13", "2026-11-08T21"] }

steps.label: every 15 min: build touched hours
steps.detail: Curated tables are rebuilt in batch rather than in the streaming job, so aggregates can be recomputed whole for every hour that received late events, and the step can be rerun or backfilled the same way.

steps.label: read new snapshots, overwrite hours on an audit branch
steps.detail: An incremental read returns only rows added since the last processed snapshot. Overwriting whole hours, instead of adding to them, makes the job idempotent: running it twice gives the same table.

steps.label: run checks on the branch
steps.detail: Checks run against the unpublished data: volume against the same hour in the last 4 weeks, null and range checks on key columns, unique keys, and that totals match the cleaned table. A failing check stops the publish, so dashboards keep showing the last good data.
steps.payload:
checks: curated.page_views_hourly @ audit_88121
  row_count vs 4-week same-hour median: -3%   (limit +-25%)   PASS
  null product_id:                      0.00% (limit 0.1%)   PASS
  unique (hour, product_id, channel):   ok                   PASS
  sum(views) = cleaned page_view count: ok                   PASS

steps.label: fast-forward main to the audit branch
steps.detail: Publishing is a metadata pointer swap, so readers move from the old hours to the new ones in one step and never see half a rebuild.

steps.label: main now at the audited snapshot
replace the 3 hours in the mart
steps.detail: Delete and insert by hour in one transaction keeps the warehouse load idempotent too. The mart is partitioned by day and clustered by product, which is how dashboards filter it.

steps.label: scan curated Parquet (3 hours only)
steps.detail: Iceberg metadata lists exactly which files hold those hours, so the warehouse reads a few hundred MB instead of listing or scanning the table.

steps.label: tile query: views by product, last 24 h
steps.detail: The dashboard reads the small hourly mart, not raw events, and its filter on the partition column limits the scan to two days of data.
steps.payload:
SELECT product_id, sum(views) AS views
FROM mart.page_views_hourly
WHERE hour >= now() - interval '24 hours'
GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT 50;

flows.title: Nightly orders load through CDC
flows.summary: CDC streams every change from the orders database into raw all day. At 01:00 the nightly DAG waits until the change log has passed midnight, merges the day's changes into cleaned.orders, pulls the SaaS exports, and runs dbt models and tests in the warehouse.

steps.label: read logical replication slot from last LSN
steps.detail: CDC reads the write-ahead log instead of querying tables, so it puts almost no load on checkout and it sees deletes and every intermediate update, which a nightly SELECT on updated_at would miss.

steps.label: write change files to raw/orders/ every 60 s
steps.detail: Each row carries the operation and the log position, which is what lets the merge apply changes in the order the database committed them.

steps.label: 01:00 ET: nightly_orders for 2026-11-09
steps.detail: A sensor waits until the CDC watermark has passed midnight ET plus a 15 minute grace, so the run never builds yesterday from a partial log. If CDC is behind, the DAG waits rather than publishing short numbers.

steps.label: submit orders_merge on a transient cluster
steps.detail: Batch jobs get their own short-lived cluster sized for the job, so they never compete with the streaming job and cost nothing between runs.

steps.label: read change files for the window
steps.detail: The window is by log position, from the LSN the last successful run stopped at to the watermark, so a rerun reads exactly the same changes.

steps.label: keep the last change per order_id by LSN
steps.detail: Files can arrive out of order and CDC can resend changes after a restart, so ordering by LSN, not by file time, makes the merge correct and repeatable.

steps.label: MERGE INTO cleaned.orders
steps.detail: The merge applies inserts, updates and deletes in one Iceberg commit, so cleaned.orders matches the database as of the watermark.
steps.payload:
MERGE INTO cleaned.orders t
USING (SELECT * FROM latest_changes) s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.lsn > t.lsn THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' THEN INSERT *;

steps.label: GET ad spend export for 2026-11-09
steps.detail: SaaS exports are pulled with an incremental cursor and backoff on rate limits. Vendors change formats without notice, which is why these files are checked against a contract before they go further.

steps.label: check against the ad_spend contract
steps.detail: The contract lists required columns, types and allowed values, so a renamed column fails here instead of silently loading as nulls.

steps.label: write raw file + overwrite cleaned day
steps.detail: The original file is kept in raw; the cleaned table's partition for the day is overwritten, so pulling the export again replaces it rather than doubling it.

steps.label: dbt build in a staging schema
steps.detail: dbt models are built into a staging schema and tested there; only when every test passes are they swapped into the schema dashboards read. That is the same write, audit, publish idea as in the lake.

steps.label: read cleaned.orders, changed partitions only
steps.detail: fct_orders is incremental: it rebuilds only the order dates touched by last night's changes, including old orders refunded yesterday.

steps.label: 214 tests, then swap staging into prod
steps.detail: Tests include unique and not-null keys, accepted status values, and a reconciliation: yesterday's revenue must match the orders database's own daily total within 0.1%.

flows.title: Upstream schema change: quarantine, alert, backfill
flows.summary: A mobile release sends add_to_cart with a changed field and an unregistered schema. Nothing is lost, because the collector accepts everything and raw keeps it; the streaming job quarantines the bad events, the quality gate keeps curated tables at the last good data, and after the fix a backfill rebuilds the affected hours.

steps.label: POST /v1/events from app 8.2
steps.detail: Release 8.2 renamed product_id to sku and sends price as text, under schema add_to_cart/4, which was never registered. The app team's CI did not run the schema compatibility check.

steps.label: produce as usual
steps.detail: The collector does not validate, so the app gets a 202 and deletes its buffer. That is deliberate: the event is safely stored and can be repaired later, whereas a rejected event would be gone.

steps.label: micro-batch: 31% of add_to_cart on /4
steps.detail: The streaming job sees the new schema reference within a minute of the release rollout reaching users.

steps.label: get schema add_to_cart/4
steps.detail: The job asks whether this version exists and is compatible with the table it feeds.

steps.label: split: valid to cleaned, failing to quarantine
steps.detail: One bad event type must not stop the whole pipeline, so the job keeps landing valid events and routes failing ones, with the reason, to a quarantine table. The gate-blocked alert opens a ticket for the platform on-call and the owning app team.

steps.label: append raw, cleaned (valid) and quarantine
13:15 curated build
steps.detail: The curated build runs on schedule; it has no idea anything is wrong upstream.

steps.label: write cart hours to an audit branch
check fails: add_to_cart volume -31%
steps.detail: Even without the quarantine signal, the volume check catches the drop, because a third of cart events are missing compared with the same hour in the last 4 weeks. main is not moved, so dashboards keep the last good hour and show its timestamp.
steps.payload:
row_count vs 4-week same-hour median: -31%  (limit +-25%)  FAIL
publish blocked; main stays at snapshot 77410 (12:00 hour)

steps.label: FAILED: gate blocked, not retried
steps.detail: Data failures are not retried automatically, since rerunning on the same bad input fails the same way. The cart dashboard goes stale, and after 30 minutes the freshness alert pages.

steps.label: register add_to_cart/4 with a mapping
steps.detail: The app team ships 8.2.1 that sends a numeric price again, and registers /4 through CI with the compatibility check now enforced. For the events already sent, the platform adds a one-off mapping: sku to product_id, and the price text parsed into amount and currency.

steps.label: trigger backfill, 13:00 to 17:00 UTC
steps.detail: A backfill is the normal job run for past hours with a parameter, not a special script, so it uses the same code, checks and publish step.

steps.label: map /4 events, overwrite cleaned and curated hours
steps.detail: Each affected hour is overwritten whole, on an audit branch, so the backfill cannot double count events that already landed and can be rerun safely if it fails halfway.
steps.payload:
INSERT OVERWRITE cleaned.events          -- hours 13..16 for add_to_cart
SELECT * FROM cleaned.events WHERE ... -- the valid /3 events already there
UNION ALL
SELECT map_v4_to_v3(payload) FROM quarantine.events
WHERE schema_ref = 'add_to_cart/4' AND hours(received_at) BETWEEN 13 AND 16;

steps.label: replace hours 13 to 16 in the marts
steps.detail: The same delete-and-insert load as every 15 minutes, for the backfilled hours. Lineage in the catalog lists every downstream table and dashboard of cleaned.events, so nothing is left with the bad numbers.

notes.text: Lake and warehouse both exist for different readers. The Iceberg lake is the system of record: cheap storage, open formats any engine can read (Spark, Trino, the warehouse itself), and the raw zone for replay. The warehouse serves BI: hundreds of concurrent short queries, caching, workload queues and fine-grained policies. A lakehouse with one engine over the lake is a reasonable simplification when BI concurrency is modest; the cost here is a copy of curated marts (40 TB) and keeping two sets of access policies in step.

Late and duplicate events are the normal case, not the exception. Partition by event time, deduplicate on event_id within a 3 day watermark, and track which hours each micro-batch touched so the curated build recomputes those hours whole. Every write overwrites a partition rather than appending to it, which is what makes reruns, retries and backfills safe.

A 1 minute streaming trigger creates 1,440 commits and many small files per table per day. Compact hourly to files of about 512 MB sorted by the most filtered columns, expire old snapshots after 7 days and remove orphan files, or query planning and scans slow down week by week. Lifecycle rules move raw files older than 30 days to infrequent access and older than 90 days to archive-instant tiers, which cuts storage for that data by roughly 40 to 70%.

PII is tagged in the catalog at the column level (email, address, user_id), and policies follow the tags: Lake Formation or BigQuery policy tags for the lake, dynamic masking in the warehouse. Cleaned tables hold a keyed hash of user_id so analysts can join and count without seeing it; only a small group can read the raw zone. A deletion request means deleting rows in every zone and then expiring the Iceberg snapshots that still reference them, or the data is still in old files.

CDC instead of nightly extracts: it sees deletes and every intermediate state, puts almost no load on the database and spreads the transfer over the day. The price is operating it: a logical replication slot keeps WAL on the production database while CDC is down, schema changes arrive as part of the stream, and an initial snapshot is needed whenever a table is added or the slot is lost.

Query cost tracks bytes scanned. A full scan of two years of cleaned events is about 150 TB, roughly $900 per query at BigQuery on-demand prices; with a 7 day partition filter it is about 1.4 TB, and reading 4 of 40 columns from clustered files brings it under 150 GB. Require partition filters on large tables, point dashboards at hourly marts instead of event tables, and set per-team budgets or reservations with alerts.

questions.q: Why have both a lake and a warehouse? Would a lakehouse alone be enough?
questions.a: The lake is the cheap, open system of record: every source lands there, raw data is kept for replay, and data scientists use Spark on it directly. The warehouse is tuned for many concurrent BI queries, with caching, workload isolation and mature fine-grained security. A lakehouse, an open table format like Iceberg queried by one engine, can serve both when BI concurrency is modest, and it removes the extra copy and the second set of policies; the trade-off is weaker concurrency and governance in some engines, and two systems means two places for access rules to drift.

questions.q: Merchandising wants the dashboards to be 1 minute behind instead of 30. What would you change, and what does it cost?
questions.a: The 30 minutes come from the 15 minute curated schedule plus the warehouse load, not from ingestion, which is already a minute behind. Getting to a minute means computing the aggregates in the stream (Flink, Dataflow or Spark streaming with event-time windows) and writing to a store built for fresh queries, which brings state management, harder handling of late events and many tiny commits. A middle way is a separate real-time view for the few metrics that need it, from the stream with approximate numbers, while the batch path stays the corrected source of truth.

questions.q: An app team renames a field in an event. How does the platform handle schema changes without breaking dashboards?
questions.a: Producers register every schema version, and the registry enforces a compatibility mode (backward: new readers can read old data), so adding an optional field passes and renaming or retyping a field is rejected, ideally in the app's CI before release. At runtime the streaming job checks each event's version, quarantines unknown or incompatible ones, and keeps the rest flowing, while raw keeps everything for a repair. Iceberg itself handles additive table changes by column id, so adding or renaming a column does not rewrite data; a real breaking change becomes a new event version with a mapping to the old shape.

questions.q: Who owns data quality, and what stops bad data from reaching the CFO's revenue dashboard?
questions.a: Producers own their contracts: the team that emits an event or owns the orders database is told when it breaks one, because only it can fix the cause. The platform owns the gates: every curated table is written to an audit branch or staging schema, checked for volume, nulls, uniqueness and reconciliation against the source, and only then published, so a failure leaves the last good data in place. The consumers of a mart own its business tests, like revenue matching finance's totals, and a blocked gate is visible as a stale timestamp rather than a wrong number.

questions.q: How do you let data scientists use clickstream and order data without exposing customer PII, and how do you honor a deletion request?
questions.a: Classify PII columns in the catalog and drive access from those tags: raw is readable by a small platform group, cleaned holds a keyed hash of user_id so joins and counts still work, and the warehouse masks email and address unless the role is allowed. Lineage shows where each PII column flows, so new tables inherit the right tags. A deletion has to reach every zone and the warehouse: delete by user, rewrite the affected files, and expire old Iceberg snapshots, otherwise time travel still returns the data.

questions.q: The warehouse bill doubled last month. How do you find the cause and keep it down?
questions.a: Start from the query log: bytes scanned or slot time by user, dashboard and table usually shows a few queries doing most of the spending, often a dashboard tile or notebook scanning an event table without a partition filter. Fix those with partition pruning (require a filter on large tables), clustering on the columns people filter by, and marts or materialized aggregates for dashboards. Then add guardrails: per-team budgets or reservations, maximum bytes per query, result caching, and storage tiering in the lake for data that is rarely read.
